speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Left unchecked, they can destroy our reputation as a trusted global financial centre or lead to terrorist attacks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We are strongly committed to combating these threats and making sure they do not take root here.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We closely supervise our banking and trading systems to prevent them from being exploited and have tough legislation and regulations which we strictly enforce.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2016, we convicted six foreign nationals for terrorism financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, we will need to strengthen our defences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Money laundering and terrorism financing are getting harder to tackle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With banking and financial systems going digital, monies can now be swiftly transferred between persons and across borders with minimum hassle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This opens up more channels to launder illicit funds and support terrorist activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The growing volume and complexity of financial transactions also make it harder for regulators to detect offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In particular, we are concerned with several groups exposed to the risk of money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first group comprises corporations and professional service providers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In one recent case, a foreign national paid a local corporate service provider to set up several "shell" companies in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The bank account of one of these companies was then used as a pass-through for stolen monies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The service provider should have known better than to be complicit in this scheme but was overcome by the temptation of easy money.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The second group comprises individuals in Singapore, who act as money mules for overseas organised syndicates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is where an individual is paid to simply accept money transfers into his or her bank account, and then transfer it out again, thus covering the tracks of illicit funds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The syndicates exploit the anonymity and reach of the Internet messaging tools and online banking to recruit locals to their schemes, and to move monies quickly through our financial system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Although regulations are in place, we need more severe punishments to enhance deterrence and more effectively deprive the criminals of their illicit assets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must also enhance our abilities to detect and prosecute these cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is the aim of the proposed amendments to the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act, or CDSA in short, and the Terrorism (Suppression of Financing) Act (TSOFA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have benchmarked our proposals against the practices of leading jurisdictions, such as Australia, the United States (US), the United Kingdom (UK) and Hong Kong.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have also considered international norms set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), of which we are a member.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As Members know, FATF is an intergovernmental body which develops international standards to fight money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will, first, explain the proposed amendments targeted at corporations and professional service providers who become involved with money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To strengthen deterrence, we propose to increase the penalties for these offences, some of which have not been changed since 2003.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, we will increase the penalties for not reporting suspicious transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, a person is required under the CDSA to report to the Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office (STRO) when he knows or has reason to believe that any property is linked to criminal conduct or drug dealing and comes across such information in the course of his work.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Such reporting is critical to our ability to enforce against money laundering and other crimes, as law enforcement agencies rely heavily on such intelligence to initiate and support investigations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: However, the existing penalties for not doing so are manifestly low, with a maximum fine at only $20,000.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Given the sums of money involved in such crimes, this is not sufficient as a deterrent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To illustrate, a property agent was fined this year for not filing a Suspicious Transaction Report after finding out that his client was linked to a foreign Ponzi scheme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is despite the property agent being well aware of his obligations to file the Report through guidelines and checklists issued by the Council for Estate Agencies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For this case, the client had wanted to buy a property at Sentosa Cove.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Had the sale gone through, the agent’s commission would have been in the range of hundreds of thousands of dollars.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A maximum fine of $20,000 clearly makes it a small risk to take.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: A related issue is tipping off on any investigations under CDSA or any disclosure made to the Suspicious Transactions Reporting Officer.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 13 amends section 48 to raise the maximum fine for tipping off under section 48(1) or (2) from $30,000 to $250,000.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Again, this is to ensure that higher penalties can be imposed on corporations that finance terrorist activities, for which $1 million may not be a sufficient deterrent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is also important for us to enhance penalties for not disclosing information related to terrorism financing to the Police.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 22 amends section 8 of the TSOFA to, amongst other things, raise the maximum penalties for failing to inform the Police about transactions relating to a terrorist’s property or whenever one controls or possesses such property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 23 amends section 10(1) to raise the maximum penalty for failing to disclose to the Police information which a person knows or believes might assist in preventing a terrorism financing offence or lead to the arrest, prosecution or conviction of another person for terrorism financing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The penalty increase under these offences will be tiered into three categories with differentiated punishments to reflect the differing culpability of groups that might commit such offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, individuals who come across the property or information in the course of their work, such as bankers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These individuals have a high level of culpability if they do not inform the Police, because they are bound to standards of professional conduct that require such reporting.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The last group comprises other individuals who are non-professionals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As this group is less culpable, the penalties are unchanged at the current maximum punishment of $50,000 fine and/or five years’ imprisonment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On a related matter, clause 24 increases the maximum penalties for disclosing information that might compromise a terrorism financing investigation under section 10B(1) and (2) to a fine of $250,000 and/or five years' imprisonment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As these offences subvert the course of justice, they should be enhanced for greater deterrence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As explained earlier, we have observed syndicates targeting locals and using their bank accounts to launder criminal proceeds.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Money laundering operations planned by these syndicates are complex, with multiple money mules being used to make it difficult for the crime proceeds to be traced to their original source.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some money mules are even trained not to make any admission during Police investigations and taught to destroy evidence by deleting handphone messages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under our current laws, the prosecution must prove that these money mules know the monies are linked to criminal conduct.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is challenging, especially against mules trained to claim ignorance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 11 introduces a new section 47AA to CDSA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This criminalises the possession or use by an accused of property which would be suspected by a reasonable person of being benefits from criminal conduct, if the accused cannot satisfactorily explain how he came by the property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: With this amendment, the Courts will be able to decide, based on the circumstances of the case, whether the accused could be reasonably expected to suspect that monies are linked to criminal conduct.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will now move on to the other proposed amendments to CDSA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While we have levers today to prosecute money laundering that is linked to overseas crimes, our law enforcement agencies have highlighted challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, prosecutors must not only prove that the overseas act amounts to a serious offence if committed in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In addition, they must also show that the overseas act amounts to an offence in the overseas jurisdiction.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is based on the established principle of dual criminality.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Practically, the law today requires prosecutors to obtain a certificate from the foreign government or a testimony from an expert in that foreign law to fulfil the burden of proof.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: First, we frequently encounter delays to obtain the certificate as the foreign government may not act on our request expeditiously, or, in some cases, may not be willing to issue it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Second, engaging an expert is costly and may discourage prosecutors from proceeding with enforcement action.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 12 amends section 47A to address these challenges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In effect, clause 12 will allow the Courts to decide on the basis of evidence presented by the Prosecution that an offence has, indeed, been committed in the overseas jurisdiction, without having to rely on foreign governments or experts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also amend our laws to strengthen our levers against Cross Border Cash Reporting Regime (CBCRR) offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under sections 48C(2) and 48E(2) of CDSA, a person is required to declare to the authorities any sum of monies brought into or out of Singapore exceeding the prescribed amount, which is $20,000 today.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Failure to make a report constitutes a CBCRR offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This gives the Court greater discretion to impose heavier penalties for CBCRR cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will bring our penalties in line with jurisdictions like the US.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For the less serious CBCRR cases, the Police have the powers to compound in lieu of prosecution.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These proposed amendments allow a wider range of penalties and composition fines to be taken against CBCRR breaches of different severity and are in line with standards set by FATF.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, we will also amend CDSA to enhance the sharing of financial intelligence with financial intelligence units of overseas jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As money laundering offences are often transnational, the exchange of financial intelligence between jurisdictions is critical to support the investigation of these cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Currently, the law only allows us to exchange intelligence with countries with which we have bilateral arrangements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We have around 50 such arrangements today with other countries’ financial intelligence units.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Clause 6 amends section 41 to allow us to exchange information under an international arrangement, provided that there are sufficient safeguards to protect the confidentiality of information shared and control their use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will be able to access more valuable information, while being assured that information shared in return is not abused, through the guidelines that the Egmont Group puts in place for its members.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Under CDSA, we will also make amendments with clauses 2 and 3 to clarify the powers of the Courts to confiscate criminal proceeds, and an amendment with clause 4 to expand the types of assets for which charging orders can be imposed on by the Courts to include “capital market products”.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will next touch on the other TSOFA amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: While cases of terrorism financing in Singapore are few, these proposed amendments are important to strengthen the counter terrorism financing regime.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This gives effect to Resolution 2178 (2014) of the Security Council of the United Nations (UN) and is also in line with FATF standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Next, we will enhance TSOFA penalties for greater deterrence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These acts are no less egregious than the primary terrorism financing offence and should be punished at the same level to create a clear deterrence against anyone from getting involved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This proposed amendment will align how we peg our terrorism financing penalties with jurisdictions like the UK and Australia.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We will also make amendments with clauses 17, 18 and 19 to protect a person against civil liability when the person complies with TSOFA prohibitions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will give greater confidence to a person to do the right thing without fear of breaching contractual obligations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These threats are real and can lead to concomitant terrorist attacks, a loss in reputation as a trusted global hub, and a breakdown in law and order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must do all that we can to obviate these risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: These proposed amendments enhance the effectiveness of our laws to deter corporations and professional service providers against being involved in money laundering and terrorism financing activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They also demonstrate our commitment that we have towards combating overseas organised syndicates and dismantling their money laundering operations involving money mules.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: All in all, the proposed amendments strengthen our frameworks to combat such criminal activities and ensure that we will have an even more effective set of levers and powers to deter, detect and prosecute.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because the present and rapid advancement of technology has facilitated the exchanging of cash for virtual currency and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Technology has also enabled transactions and transfers to be done from almost anywhere.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, someone who does not have an e-payment app could easily ask someone else to help them pay another person in exchange for the money in cash.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would not normally be a problem unless the cash actually came, for instance, from dealing in drugs or other illicit activities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, clause 4 expands the definition of capital market products, no longer requiring the product to be linked to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This allows a charging order to be made against more assets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The other crime that this Bill strengthens our stance against is the financing of terrorism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It adds financial support to aid the committing of heinous acts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, terrorism financing has to be stopped and its streams of support dried up.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To that end, Singapore is party to the International Convention for the Suppression of the Financing of Terrorism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: TSOFA implements this international agreement and, today, this Bill goes further in our commitment by implementing the UN Security Council Resolution 2178 through clause 18.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 21 goes one step further and makes it an offence to abet, attempt or conspire to commit those terrorism financing offences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because people would not be convicted of a crime without fulfilling both the mental element and physical action of the offence, there may be instances where although they were unaware, acts of terrorism are still being financially supported.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, may I ask the Minister: what is being done to raise awareness on what are some "red flags" to look out for, such that monies donated or provided do not unwittingly fund terrorism?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides expanding the scope of offences, this Bill also makes enforcement and investigation easier under CDSA, an Act that the Minister alluded to in her speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By facilitating the sharing of information internationally and by making it easier to prove that something is a foreign serious offence or foreign drug offence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, knowledge and information are key assets in winning wars against terror as well as its financing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The third way in which this Bill strengthens our response to transnational financial crimes is by enhancing penalties.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because these financial crimes are calculated crimes based on the lucrativeness and perceived benefit of committing a crime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, it is imperative that Singapore plays its part by deploying tough laws to deter money laundering and financing of terrorism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, would the Minister share with us how the proposed punishment tariffs compare with other jurisdictions and how the punishment tariffs in this Bill were calculated?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe the Minister talked about how the punishment tariffs were calculated in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am asking how they compare with the other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was stated that the Bill would enable Singapore to more effectively tackle money laundering and terrorism financing, which are usually more complex and transnational in nature.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Ministry emphasised that there was a need to ensure that our laws remained relevant to the current operating landscape.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One gets the sense that this Bill is being tabled because the current laws are deemed somewhat inadequate to deal with the problem of money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, the ongoing investigations into the 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) scandal and the alleged transfers of hundreds of millions of dollars to and from the Singapore bank accounts of Mr Low Taek Jho, or Jho Low, make uneasy reading.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: An online financial news portal finews.asia has even described Singapore as, and I quote, "the banking centre at the heart of the scandal".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the facts are yet to be fully established, this is a reputation we do not want.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I thus support moves to strengthen the legal and enforcement machinery to tackle this challenging task.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To have a further understanding of the need to amend our laws, could the Government share its assessment of the current efficacy of the two Acts in question, namely, CDSA and TSOFA?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What has been the rate of reporting, detection and prosecution, and how satisfactory is it?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the Bill now before the House, I note that the Bill focuses much attention on enhancing the penalties for offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such illicit activities will go on unless the chance of being caught is high.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Here, the law enforcement agencies face a monumental task.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides their transnational nature, laundering criminal proceeds and financing terrorism usually involve layers of intermediaries, including seemingly innocuous ones like legitimate businesses and charities, making detection especially challenging.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, the Minister also mentioned anonymous digital transfers as yet another obstacle for investigators to overcome today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this vein, I would like to seek some clarification as to how the Government as a whole is going about improving the likelihood of detection of such activities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such an endeavour will involve other authorities and agencies besides the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Last year, it was announced that the Government was going on the offensive against money laundering and terrorism financing by setting up the Anti-Money laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism Industry Partnership (ACIP), under the auspices of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Commercial Affairs Department (CAD).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The ACIP would specifically work with eight banks and the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One year on, how has it enhanced the likelihood of detection of such crimes?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides domestic agencies, the sharing of financial intelligence across borders is vital.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would be useful for the Minister to give her assessment on how well the current bilateral arrangements are working, and to elaborate further on the potential of working with countries who have subscribed to the Egmont Documents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In summary, Sir, I believe the Bill brings about important changes which are necessary to meet the challenge of tackling money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, the Government's clarifications on improving detection and the effectiveness of financial intelligence sharing will be most relevant to the Bill's efficacy.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We have trusted reputation as a financial, business and economic centre.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our regulatory framework is current and relatively robust but there may be loopholes.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Moreover, money laundering and terrorism funding these days are getting more sophisticated and it may go undetected for some time.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Being linked to different aspects of terrorism today seems to be sexy and fashionable, especially for certain segments of people and perhaps also our young who may view it as an exciting adventure.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I have a few clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How is it different from the usual enforcement officers?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As their jobs entail getting and procuring information with foreign countries as well, how are these officers identified and trained?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How are they different from the usual CAD?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How do we stand in the implementation of the recommended regulations and guidelines thus far?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What are these so far and how have we worked to ensure they are addressed appropriately and adequately and are reviewed at regular intervals?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thirdly, also pertaining to FATF, there is a recommendation on preventing abuse of non-profit organisations and the non-government organisation (NGO) sector.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Globally, this sector seems to be at a higher risk for money laundering and terrorist funding activities.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can the Minister share on how we have ringfenced and conducted surveillance on these as necessary?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fourthly, on matters pertaining to money laundering and counter-terrorism funding, it requires a national and concerted effort.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Whilst the financial sector may be more well prepared and vigilant as it is often a target sector, how about our other non-financial sectors and stakeholders?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fifth, in line with this Bill, we may also need to strengthen and have more prudent risk assessment when dealing with foreign businesses and investments.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How are we educating and aligning our business personnel, trade sectors and also how is the Ministry working perhaps with our chambers of commerce.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   I have two questions for the Minister in relation to this Bill.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: First, regarding this Bill, can the Minister provide clarification on the sharing of cross-border information through the officers who are tasked with the issue of terrorism funding?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How does the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) provide guidance and heighten awareness amongst our Mosque Management Boards so that they have a better understanding and become more vigilant about their financial account matters?

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): There is a need for us to develop a culture of risk sensitivity through better risk assessment.

speaker: Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: All stakeholders across all industries must work hand-in-hand to uphold our reputation and combat the potential undesirable effects of a possibility that is waiting to happen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given Singapore’s position as a major financial hub and the greater push towards digitisation of our financial services and banking industry, Singapore is vulnerable to criminals who exploit our financial system to make illicit gains.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There has been a trend of rising economic crime worldwide.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In response to a Parliamentary Question that I filed last month on economic crimes in Singapore, the hon Minister for Home Affairs stated that the number of commercial crimes reported in Singapore had remained stable over the last three years from 2015 to 2017.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, in PwC's global economic crime and fraud survey 2018, PwC noted its findings of a sharp increase and a record high of reported economic crime in Singapore, which is consistent with the global trend.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, according to PwC's survey, more than one-third of Singapore-based organisations experienced economic crime, up from 22% in 2016.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Attorney-General noted in his keynote address at the 36th Cambridge International Symposium on Economic Crime earlier this year that while our domestic crime rate remains low, Singapore’s exposure to transnational economic crime is on the rise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the increase in both extent and sophistication of transnational economic crime syndicates, I fully support the Bill, which seeks to enhance the law enforcement agencies' abilities to seize assets from illicit activities and deter criminals by taking the profit out of their crimes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I beg to differ with the opinion expressed by the hon Member of Parliament Ms Sylvia Lim who postulated the question as to whether this Bill throws up purported inadequacies in the current regime by reference to the 1MDB case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a private practitioner, it seems to me that actually the 1MDB case shows the efficacy of the regime as it stands now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore, ahead of other jurisdictions, has prosecuted and secured convictions of perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, two banks were closed down as the result of quick action by the relevant law enforcement authorities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Not only that, recently, FATF has given Singapore, after a mutual evaluation, a clean bill of health.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, this shows that the regime works but we are faced with a dynamic situation, not a static situation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And it is entirely appropriate for the hon Minister to highlight that, given the inventiveness of these criminals, we need to constantly check to see whether or not the measures we have are adequate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I have a few suggestions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Bill provides for the Public Prosecutor to apply to Court to make a confiscation order against monies that a person has moved in or out of Singapore in contravention of section 48C or 48D of CDSA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This, as well as confiscation powers under sections 4 and 5 of CDSA, only apply after the accused is convicted of the offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By then, it may be too late as the monies may have been dissipated by the accused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These provisions will have "bite" if assets are frozen at the outset and the confiscation order is then applied against the frozen assets.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There could also be situations where assets from ill-gotten gains are in Singapore, given that it is a prominent international financial centre.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, the prosecution, much less conviction, is not contemplated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Yet, there is a compelling case to seize and confiscate such monies, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Act, which was introduced in 2016, allows for confiscation without the need for a criminal conviction where a person carries out a serious offence at the direction of an organised criminal group.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Serious offences include the various offences under CDSA, such as assisting to retain, acquiring, possessing or transferring benefits of criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the Organised Crime Act, as the name implies, requires the prosecutor to prove that the accused knew or had reasonable grounds to believe that he or she was acting in accordance with the direction of an organised criminal group.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Providing for a wider civil-based freezing and confiscation regime under CDSA would give the law enforcement agencies more teeth.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a parallel, the US has a civil forfeiture regime in place, which allows law enforcement officers to take assets from persons suspected of involvement in crime, without necessarily charging them for wrongdoing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Australia also has a similar legislation which allows for civil-based recovery.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such civil-based recovery allows restraint and recovery of assets suspected of criminal origins without the necessity of securing a criminal conviction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The UK Law Commission has recently embarked on a two-year project to review its laws on confiscation to ensure effective recovery of proceeds of crime which is presently in the pre-consultation stage.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The review will focus on whether the present conviction-based confiscation regime is sufficient and what improvements could be made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is typical, in the words of Prof Michael Levi, a very well-known criminology professor, that criminals in such situations often claim that they have spent all their ill-gotten gains on fast women and slow horses.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Clearly though, they should not be taken at face value.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should ensure that we have sufficient tools to combat economic crimes, in particular, by depriving criminals of their ill-gotten gains.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard and in light of the global trends, I have three suggestions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, providing for an increase in punishment or some punitive measure against the criminal if the confiscation order made against him is not satisfied.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is already a trend in the UK of unsatisfied confiscation orders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such paper judgments cannot deter people from committing economic crimes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What we do not want is for criminals to go to jail at the expense of our people, come out and then connect with the monies that they had stolen later.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, providing resources to our authorities to "chase" after the assets of criminals in other countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It should not just stop at invoking Mutual Legal Aid Treaties (MLATs).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If necessary, there should be civil actions taken to recover the proceeds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will allow the confiscation order that may be made subsequently in the event of a conviction to have more "bite".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my Parliamentary Question last month on economic crimes, I had asked for the total value of assets misappropriated or gained by offenders who have been convicted for economic crimes in Singapore, in contrast with the total value of assets recovered by the authorities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Without tracking such data, we may not be able to monitor the effectiveness of our confiscation regime to track our progress on this front.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Separately, I would ask how would the confiscation orders work in the context of co-accused persons?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would they be jointly and severally liable in respect of the confiscation order?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Apart from this, what other international arrangements are contemplated, and would such international arrangements be disclosed?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The confiscation provisions in the Bill specifically focuses on the final "D" is deprivation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My suggestions are made in the context of focusing also on the first two Ds, that is, getting the authorities to detect the extent of a criminal’s wealth as well as providing some "teeth" to deter like-minded offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As criminals constantly revamp their methods to evade detection and the law, we, too, must constantly evaluate our means to guard against them or deter such behaviour.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the Bill, which is in step with our efforts to ensure that Singapore is not seen as an easy target for criminals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members raised many useful points, which I will address.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked how we are regulating non-profit organisations, businesses and professions, such as law and accountancy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: She also asked how MUIS is working with the management of mosques to ensure that they do not run afoul of our laws on anti-money laundering and countering terrorism financing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked how we are raising awareness of such laws so that monies donated or provided are not unwittingly used to fund terrorism.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Professionals in non-financial sectors that may be at risk of becoming parties to money laundering activities, such as lawyers, accountants and so on, are collectively known as Designated Non-Financial Business Professionals (DNFBPs).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are many, many acronyms in this particular set of amendments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, the different DNFBPs are supervised by their respective sector regulators.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, casinos are supervised by the Casino Regulatory Authority (CRA), and corporate service providers by the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These regulators develop the control measures to address their sector's inherent risks against money laundering and terrorism financing and oversee implementation of these requirements through education and enforcement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Examples of such requirements include the need for DNFBPs to put in place customer due diligence measures and to have controls and policies to ensure compliance with UN sanctions obligations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: DNFBPs who breach these requirements are liable to a range of penalties, including fines or face prosecution.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the non-profit sector, charities are supervised by the Charities Unit, and mosques by MUIS.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These agencies work closely with charities and mosques to educate them about their risks and help them to put in place procedures to identify and report suspicious transactions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: At the national level, MHA, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) and MAS have set up the Steering Committee for combating money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This Steering Committee formulates our national policies on anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) to ensure that our mechanisms and controls against money laundering and terrorism financing remain relevant and are consistent with international standards and best practices.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It also coordinates the practices of regulatory and law enforcement agencies in different sectors to ensure consistency.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our coordinated national approach has strengthened our regime.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked for the rate of reporting, detection and prosecution of CDSA and TSOFA cases, and how the setting up of ACIP has enhanced the detection of such cases.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We strive to improve the situation further through ACIP, which brings together stakeholders from industry and the Government to discuss and raise awareness of transnational financial risks confronting Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Since it began in 2017, it has published two papers highlighting best practices regarding red flag indicators and crime typologies targeted at businesses and professions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The papers guide industries to put in place better controls to detect financial crimes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police are also sharing case-specific information with ACIP stakeholders to help them better detect and report crime.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The increase in STRs filed over the past few years suggests that the different sectors are increasingly aware of their AML and CFT obligations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Sector agencies regulating DNFBPs also observed the improving quality of such reports.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked specifically how we stand in the implementation of FATF standards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: FATF member countries, such as Singapore, go through periodic assessments to assess our compliance with the standards, and whether our measures are effective.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The last assessment on Singapore in 2016 showed that we have a strong regulatory framework, good understanding of our risks and good internal cooperation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nevertheless, we have to anticipate and strengthen our defences.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In areas where there were suggestions for improvement, we have taken firm action.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, FATF highlighted the need to enhance transparency of information on beneficial ownership for companies, limited liability partnerships and trustees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In 2017, we amended our laws to require such entities to maintain beneficial ownership information.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOF and ACRA are exploring the setting up of a central non-public register of such information, where timely access will facilitate law enforcement and supervisory efforts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another area FATF highlighted was the need to regulate the precious stones and metal dealers (PSMDs).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Since then, the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) has established a new AML and CFT Division.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, MinLaw recently concluded a public consultation on the proposed regulatory regime for PSMDs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali Pillai was accurate in categorising this set of amendments as anticipatory in nature so that we do not find ourselves on the back foot in a dynamic anti-money laundering and counter terrorism financing landscape.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He suggested strengthening our powers of confiscation and shared a number of practices across international jurisdictions which allow confiscation to take place prior to or apart from criminal proceedings, such as civil confiscation regimes, unexplained wealth orders and freezing orders.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During investigations, the Police can seize the property under section 35 of the Criminal Procedure Code if it is suspected to be linked to a criminal offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, section 16 of CDSA allows the High Court to make a restraint order on the property of an accused involved in these crimes even if the property might not be directly linked to these crimes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These levers allow the Court to subsequently confiscate the property once the accused is convicted, minimising the risk of dissipation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In determining the confiscation amount upon conviction, law enforcement agencies will consider the criminal's known income.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Similar to the unexplained wealth order regime in the UK, any amount that is disproportionate to his known income will be presumed to have been derived benefits from criminal conduct and confiscated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Murali Pillai also had specific questions about how confiscation works.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Regarding his question on whether we should have punitive measures against the criminal if the confiscation order made against him is not satisfied, section 14 of CDSA allows us to do that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In effect, it converts the outstanding amount into equivalent fines and allows the Court to imprison the person in default for not paying the fine.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He also asked how confiscation orders would work in the context of a co-accused.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Confiscation is pursued against an individual, and not jointly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With the above measures in place, we assess that there is currently no need for a civil confiscation regime under CDSA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But let me assure Mr Murali Pillai that this is a matter we will continue to review.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On international benchmarks, Mr Christopher de Souza asked how our penalties compare with other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The increased penalties allow for greater deterrence against such offences and are benchmarked to international standards.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For the amendment cited by Mr Christopher de Souza in which we are raising the penalty for an individual failing to file STRs from a fine of $20,000 to a maximum penalty of a fine of $250,000 and/or imprisonment of up to three years, the revised penalties are comparable with jurisdictions, such as New Zealand and the US, where fines can go up to S$300,000 and imprisonment in the range of two to five years.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In most cases, including the case of failing to file STRs, we have increased or tiered the penalties to allow a calibrated response according to the severity of the offence and the nature of the offender.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, the maximum penalty imposed on a corporation is higher than on an individual.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also sought to achieve parity across the penalties in CDSA and TSOFA based on the nature of the offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, the penalties for persons failing to report information on terrorism financing is pegged to the penalties for failing to file an STR.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is because, in both cases, there is a similar professional obligation on persons to report suspicious information or transactions to the authorities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Next, let me address international cooperation and its effectiveness, which Prof Fatimah Lateef and Ms Sylvia Lim asked about.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef also asked about the role and training of officers from STRO.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: STRO is a specialised unit in CAD of the Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: STRO officers gather intelligence from a variety of sources to detect financial crime and support investigations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As STRO manages sensitive information, all its officers are security-vetted and undergo comprehensive training on their responsibilities in managing such information.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides the STRs, as mentioned in my earlier speech, STRO officers also work closely with foreign counterparts to exchange intelligence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Cooperation with overseas jurisdictions has led us to detect transnational crime and prevent our financial systems from being abused.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We were able to seize the criminal proceeds and successfully return the monies to the country of origin.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Depriving overseas syndicates of their criminal proceeds deters them from using Singapore to launder their ill-gotten gains.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The growing volume and complexity of financial transactions across borders point to the increasing importance of international cooperation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In my earlier opening speech, I shared with Members how our proposed amendments will allow us to exchange financial intelligence, including information on terrorism financing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will open up new channels of information and allow us to more effectively target overseas organised syndicates and their money mule operations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Murali Pillai's question on whether the Government is contemplating other international arrangements, we are always open to possibilities but have no firm plans for now.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope I have addressed their concerns adequately.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Money laundering and terrorism financing are serious crimes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With the support of the House, I beg to move.
